passage_title: The Complaint Book of Brandt's Ferry
passage:
[1] In 1884 the water board of Brandt's Ferry received sixty-one written complaints about the municipal supply. In 1889 it received four hundred and three. The board's own minutes for that year call the increase "a plain index of deterioration in the works," and the sentence has been quoted ever since by people writing the sanitary history of the valley. It is the natural reading. It is also, I will argue, wrong in a way worth more than the correction.

[2] The board kept sample sheets, and they survive: twelve readings a month, three apiece at a single hydrant in each of four wards, the sixteen wards taken in rotation so that every ward's hydrant was read in three months of the year. The clerk entered the results under a column headed "sediment" and a second headed "odour, on a scale of five." By the board's own measures the water improved steadily across exactly the years in which the complaints multiplied. The sediment figure for the Ferry Street hydrant fell from nine to three between 1884 and 1889; the odour column, which never fell below four in 1884, never rose above two after 1887. Whatever the complaints were tracking, it was not the contents of the pipe.

[3] Something else changed in March 1886. The board had reported its readings to the public since 1879, but only once a year and only as a single figure for the town, printed in the year-end report and, so far as I can tell, read by almost nobody. That March the board began buying a quarter column in the Brandt's Ferry Courier every month, and the quarter column carried the sediment reading, hydrant by hydrant, for the four wards the board had sampled that month. For the first time a resident of Ferry Street could find a number that belonged to Ferry Street and to no other street.

[4] Complaints did not follow the water. They followed the column. Because the rotation brought each ward round three times a year, every ward's figure appeared three times in the first twelve months of the arrangement; and in fourteen of the sixteen wards the peak month for complaints in those twelve months was the month directly after that ward's figure had appeared for the first time, and not the month after its second appearance or its third. Two wards break the pattern. Both are wards whose hydrant numbers the Courier transposed in its first year of the arrangement, a fact I would much rather have found than invented.

[5] The obvious objection is that Brandt's Ferry was simply filling up. It was: the assessors' rolls give a population rise of twenty-two percent across the decade. But complaints rose more than sixfold, and the rolls allow the thing to be put per household, which is the form in which the objection dies. In 1884 roughly one household in three hundred complained. In 1889 roughly one in fifty did.

[6] A second objection deserves more patience than it is usually given. Postage fell in the same period, and reading and writing spread; perhaps what rose was not grievance but the ease of getting grievance onto paper. The board's counter clerk, however, kept a separate day-book for complaints made in person, by people who paid no postage and wrote nothing down. That book climbs on the same curve, in the same months, as the letters do.

[7] The complaints changed in kind as well, and the change is harder to explain away than the change in number. Before 1886 they are about the senses: water that "smells of the tannery," water "thick enough to see the bottom of the cup through, and no further." After 1886 a new sentence appears, and then appears constantly, in one form or another. The writer gives the printed figure for his own street and says that the water at his tap is worse than the sheet allows. He is not describing water. He is disputing a number.

[8] I would temper the conclusion before anybody repeats it. Nothing here shows that the complainants were mistaken, and some of them plainly were not; the transposed wards are proof that the sheet could be wrong about a street. The claim is narrower than that. A grievance needs a standard before it can be stated as a grievance, and the monthly column handed sixteen wards a standard they had never had. What the board manufactured in March 1886 was not dirty water. It was the possibility of saying, with a figure to point at, that the water was dirtier than it ought to be.

[9] The board stopped buying the column in 1891, for reasons the minutes give as economy. Within a year the complaints had fallen to ninety-six, and the minutes enter that fall as evidence that the works had at last been put right. It is the most useful passage in the whole archive, and the one most often quoted for the opposite of what it shows.

passage:

[2] The board kept sample sheets, and they survive: twelve readings a month, three apiece at a single hydrant in each of four wards, the sixteen wards taken in rotation so that every ward's hydrant was read in three months of the year. The clerk entered the results under a column headed "sediment" and a second headed "odour, on a scale of five." By the board's own measures the water improved steadily across exactly the years in which the complaints multiplied. The sediment figure for the Ferry Street hydrant fell from nine to three between 1884 and 1889; the odour column, which never fell below four in 1884, never rose above two after 1887. That March the board began buying a quarter column in the Brandt's Ferry Courier every month, and the quarter column carried the sediment reading, hydrant by hydrant, for the four wards the board had sampled that month. For the first time a resident of Ferry Street could find a number that belonged to Ferry Street and to no other street.

In 1889 roughly one in fifty did.

Postage fell in the same period, and reading and writing spread; perhaps what rose was not grievance but the ease of getting grievance onto paper. passage:
[1] On the Menara Flats the beetle Peraphes arida spends most of its life as an egg. The eggs lie in the top four centimetres of a salt-crusted clay pan, and they can lie there for six years. The first heavy rain of the wet season does nothing to them: we have watched forty-one first rains and recorded a hatch after none of them. The second rain hatches them, and it does so quickly, between thirty and fifty hours after the water arrives.

[2] The account we inherited, and taught, was cumulative. An egg needs a certain total of water before it can develop, the reasoning went, and one storm on the Flats rarely delivers that total while two usually do. The account had the merit of explaining why the gap between the two rains seemed not to matter much, and it fitted the rough arithmetic: the mean first rain on the Flats drops eleven millimetres and the mean second drops nine, and twenty millimetres is close to the figure at which the pans begin to hold standing water.

[3] It is also testable in a tray, which is what we did. Ninety trays of pan clay, two hundred eggs in each, twenty-four millimetres of water to each tray over one week. Half the trays received that water in a single pour. Half received it as two pours of twelve millimetres, three days apart. The clay, the eggs, the total water and the week were the same in both groups.

[4] The single-pour trays produced nine larvae in all. The two-pour trays produced more than three thousand. We ran the same design at eighteen, at twenty-four and at thirty-one degrees, because warmth is the other thing a first rain brings, and the spread across those three temperatures was too small for us to tell them apart; the spread between one pour and two was the entire result.

[5] What is different about the second pour is the water that leaves it. The Flats carry a salt crust, thin and white and reliably present by the end of the dry season. The first water to fall dissolves that crust, and the pore water an egg is sitting in during a first rain is briny: our probes read fourteen grams of salt per litre in the hour after a first pour. By the second pour the crust is gone and its salt has drained away with the first water, and the same probes read two.

[6] So we ran the experiment the other way round. One set of trays took two pours of brine matched to the fourteen-gram reading, and gave nineteen larvae. A second set took one pour of brine and then one of fresh water, and gave better than two thousand. A third set took no first pour at all. We salted the surface of the clay, left it to dry until a crust had formed, and then lifted that crust away whole before giving the trays a single pour of twelve millimetres of fresh water; the probes read two, and the set hatched almost as well as the two-pour group had, on half the water. The egg is not counting rains. It is waiting for the salt to fall.

[7] Why an egg should wait for that, we can only propose. A single storm can wet the Flats without filling them, and the shallow pans a larva needs fill only after the clay has taken up its own first water; a larva has eleven days and cannot leave the pan it hatches in. Fresh pore water may be the most reliable sign available underground that the surface has already been rinsed once. We say may. Nothing in our trays tests what happens in a pan, and an adaptive story is the easiest kind to tell and the hardest to hold yourself to.

[8] There is one check on all of this that we did not design, and it is the neighbouring population on the Sharra ridge, forty kilometres east and eighty metres higher, where the runoff carries the salt off each year and no crust forms. Those beetles hatch on the first rain. That is the result our account predicts. We are also aware that it is the result a dozen other accounts predict, since the ridge differs from the Flats in altitude, in clay and in the length of its dry season as well as in salt.

[9] The experiment that would settle the matter is unglamorous, and we have not yet been given leave to run it: lay a salt crust by hand over a measured stretch of the ridge and see whether the beetles there stop hatching on the first rain. If they hatch anyway, the account in this paper is finished, whatever the trays say. We would rather write that sentence than let the trays stand in for the Flats.
